description:
Aspirational benchmark ideas that are not yet ready for implementation. When an idea is ready, create a dedicated tracker item with full tasks, decision gates, guardrails, and acceptance criteria, then mark it here as promoted.

Re-triaged 2026-09-25. Each entry below records its status and dated evidence. The legacy work units (w1-w12) in this item's `legacy` section predate this triage. Use the status map here, not the legacy `pending` flags.

## Status map for the legacy work units
- w1-w4 (graph benchmark: Neo4j/Neptune, LDBC SNB, query-language strategy, workload): **split**. The SQL-expressible part is ready to promote (see 'Promote now'). Native graph engines stay here.
- w5-w8 (interactive benchmark explorer web UI): **superseded, done elsewhere**. BenchBox ships the Results Explorer (`results-explorer/`: Preact + Vite + DuckDB-WASM, static, no server API), which answers w6 (users/use cases), w7 (tech stack: no Flask/FastAPI backend), and w8 (results API: static snapshots queried in-browser). Explorer follow-ups are tracked in their own items (e.g. rework-results-secondary-navigation-information-architecture). Nothing remains here.
- w9-w12 (streaming: Kafka/Flink/Spark Streaming, Nexmark, TSBS overlap, broker vs processor): **stays in backlog**, with updated findings below.
- Geospatial: was already removed from this backlog. It is tracked as the tracker item `geospatial-primitives-benchmark`. The old path `TODO/benchmark-expansion/planning/geospatial-primitives-benchmark.yaml` no longer exists: `_project/TODO` holds only `_indexes`.

## Promote now: SQL graph analytics based on LDBC SNB BI
- LDBC's official BI repository (github.com/ldbc/ldbc_snb_bi, Apache-2.0, last pushed 2026-04-07) contains an Umbra implementation of all 20 BI queries written in PostgreSQL-dialect SQL (`umbra/queries/bi-1..20.sql`). Path queries (Q15, Q19, Q20) use `WITH RECURSIVE` bidirectional BFS, and parameters use psql `\set`, which BenchBox would substitute. No graph engine is required.
- Pre-generated datasets are on Cloudflare R2 (datasets.ldbcouncil.org/bi-pre-audit/, composite-merged-fk and projected-fk CSV formats) at SF1, 3, 10, 30, 100, 300, 1000, 3000, and 10000, with md5 checksums. Substitution parameters cover SF1-SF30000. SF10 validation outputs generated by Umbra exist for answer checking. No Spark datagen is needed.
- Fit: runs on BenchBox's existing SQL platforms, notably DuckDB, PostgreSQL, and CedarDB (Umbra's successor), and stresses recursive CTEs, deep joins, and many-to-many traversal, which TPC workloads don't cover.
- Constraints to carry into the promoted item:
  (a) Only audited results may be called 'LDBC Benchmark Results', so name it as 'derived from LDBC SNB BI'.
  (b) The dataset licence is unverified; confirm before shipping a downloader (precedent: seek-formal-legal-review-of-imdb-dataverse-terms).
  (c) Recursive-CTE support varies by platform, so gate per platform.
  (d) Validate against the published SF10 Umbra outputs, and DuckDB at SF1.

## Backlog: full-text search plus analytics on log data (SearchBench)
Source: SereneDB blog 'SearchBench vs ClickHouse' (https://serenedb.com/blog/searchbench-clickhouse), read 2026-09-25, and the repository github.com/serenedb/searchbench (Apache-2.0, last pushed 2026-09-25).

What it is:
- An open, ClickBench-style benchmark for search engines on log-shaped data.
- Data: OpenTelemetry logs from ClickHouse's TextBench, as public Parquet (`https://public-pme.s3.eu-west-3.amazonaws.com/text_bench`). Scales are 100M, 1B, 10B, and 50B rows. Smoke scales (100k, 1m, 100m) are sliced from part_000.parquet with HTTP byte-range reads, so no full ~40 GB download is needed. Schema: 15 columns including Timestamp, TraceId, SpanId, SeverityText/Number, ServiceName, Body (the full-text field), and Resource/Scope/Log attribute maps. SereneDB reports 11.2 GiB on disk at 100M rows and 112.2 GiB at 1B.
- Queries: 92. Q01-Q83 cover search and aggregation: boolean token match (term, AND, OR, negation, min-match), phrase and proximity, prefix/suffix/wildcard/regexp/fuzzy, BM25-ranked top-K, time-ordered log tailing, and GROUP BY aggregations. Q84-Q92 are joins on TraceId. Q01-Q83 are derived from TextBench (Apache-2.0), so rows can be compared with TextBench's leaderboard; the BM25 top-K queries are SearchBench additions.
- Engines in the repo: SereneDB, ClickHouse (sorted and unsorted), Elasticsearch (incl. columnar), OpenSearch, ParadeDB, vanilla Postgres FTS, TigerData (incl. columnstore), CrateDB, ArangoDB, Manticore, Quickwit, VictoriaLogs.
- Method: ClickBench-style runner (install/start/stop/check/load/query/data-size scripts per engine). GCP n2-standard-32 (32 vCPU, 128 GB RAM, 3.9 TB SSD). Three runs per query, best of the last two reported. Page cache dropped for cold runs at 1B/10B. 60 s timeout. Client round-trip timing. Single client, single node.
- Headline claim (10B rows, hot): SereneDB 173.5 ms median with 92/92 finished; ClickHouse sorted 1912.5 ms with 60/92; unsorted 2301.0 ms with 48/92. ClickHouse's text index has no BM25, so 22 queries are unsupported. Treat these as vendor-reported and unverified.

Fit for BenchBox:
- Fills a gap. BenchBox has no full-text search benchmark. vector_search covers only ANN, and ClickBench and read_primitives do no text retrieval.
- Many BenchBox platforms have native full-text or inverted indexes that no current benchmark exercises: ClickHouse text index, PostgreSQL FTS (GIN), the DuckDB fts extension, Doris/StarRocks/Databend inverted indexes, Snowflake SEARCH(), BigQuery SEARCH(), TimescaleDB, and SereneDB (planned). ParadeDB pg_search would be a new Postgres-extension candidate (see platform-expansion-evaluation-2026-09).
- Local-friendly: the smoke scales run on a laptop with no bulk download.

Blockers and design questions to settle before promoting:
(a) Queries are hand-written per engine. Full-text syntax has no common SQL: SereneDB uses `@@` and `ts_*` functions, Postgres uses `to_tsquery` over GIN, and ClickHouse uses its text-index functions. BenchBox's single-source-plus-sqlglot model doesn't apply. It would need per-platform query variants registered in sql_compat (precedent: query_source/vector_search_variants.py, nyctaxi_variants.py), plus a per-platform capability matrix with unsupported queries registered as skips.
(b) Result equivalence is hard. BM25 scores and top-K membership depend on tokenizer/analyzer settings, so exact-match validation against DuckDB won't work for ranked queries. It needs a documented contract: exact for boolean-match counts and aggregations; overlap/recall tolerance for ranked top-K. SearchBench ships `lib/check_results.py`, which is worth studying.
(c) Vendor authorship. SereneDB wrote the benchmark and its adapters, so BenchBox must own its own query variants and tuning per platform, and must not import vendor configurations as neutral defaults.
(d) Index build is part of the cost. Separate load time from index-build time, and report index size, following BenchBox's phase model.
(e) Engines without SQL (Elasticsearch, OpenSearch, Quickwit, VictoriaLogs) are out of scope unless reached through an SQL interface. BenchBox benchmarks SQL/DataFrame platforms.
(f) Scale: 1B+ rows needs over 100 GiB. Local work is limited to the smoke scales; larger scales are live-cloud or native-Linux runs and need approval.

Suggested first slice when promoted: a spike on the 100M smoke scale with DuckDB (fts), PostgreSQL (GIN FTS), ClickHouse (text index), and SereneDB. Implement boolean-match, phrase, and aggregation queries first, deferring BM25 ranking until the equivalence contract (b) is settled. Related item: serenedb-search-benchmarks (SereneDB-specific search enablement); the two should share the query-variant design.

Re-evaluate when: the SereneDB adapter lands (serenedb-adapter-core), or a user asks for text-search comparisons across BenchBox platforms.

## Stays in backlog: native graph engines and graph query languages
- GQL (ISO/IEC 39075) was published 2024-04-11. Neo4j Cypher now covers most mandatory GQL features. Neptune (openCypher/Gremlin/SPARQL) is cloud-only.
- Kùzu (embedded graph DB, a natural local candidate) was archived on 2025-10-10 after Apple acquired Kùzu Inc. Community forks exist (LadybugDB, Bighorn). Wait until a fork proves durable.
- SQL/PGQ (SQL:2023 part 16): PostgreSQL 19 committed it (2026-03-16) but reverted it on 2026-09-07. The earliest it could return is PostgreSQL 20 (about September 2027). DuckPGQ (DuckDB community extension) works but has reported compatibility limits with newer DuckDB patch releases. Oracle 23ai supports SQL/PGQ, but Oracle has no BenchBox adapter (see platform-expansion-evaluation-2026-09).
- Re-evaluate when: PostgreSQL 20 ships SQL/PGQ, DuckPGQ tracks DuckDB releases reliably, or a Kùzu fork reaches a stable release. The natural next step then is a SQL/PGQ variant of the promoted LDBC-derived workload, not a separate Cypher/Gremlin adapter family.

## Stays in backlog: streaming benchmarks (Nexmark)
- Nexmark is the de facto streaming-SQL benchmark (a 27-query set as run by RisingWave against Flink). Relevant engines: Apache Flink SQL, RisingWave and Materialize (both PostgreSQL-wire, and sqlglot ships dialects for both), and Spark Structured Streaming.
- Blocker: BenchBox measures bounded batch query timings. Streaming needs a sustained event source, continuous queries or materialized views, and throughput/latency metrics. That is a new measurement subsystem, not a benchmark add-on.
- w11 resolved: TSBS DevOps (`benchbox/tsbs_devops.py`) is batch time-series querying and does not overlap with continuous stream processing.
- w12 resolved: benchmark the processing engines (Flink, RisingWave, Materialize). Kafka is only the source and should not be benchmarked as an engine.
- Re-evaluate when there is sponsorship or user demand. A cheaper first step, if wanted: run Nexmark's queries as batch SQL over generated bounded event tables on existing platforms (no streaming semantics), clearly labeled as such.
